title: Signed lattice-path shuffle boundary identity on unnormalized free simplices
statement:
Use chain complexes of $\mathbf Z$-modules (abelian groups) as in [def-weil-pbc-module-chain-complex-homology]. Let $p,q\geq0$ be integers. For $a\geq0$, let $U(p)_a$ be the free abelian group of finite integral linear combinations of weakly increasing strings $u=(u_0,\ldots,u_a)$ with $0\leq u_i\leq p$. Set $\partial u=\sum_{i=0}^a(-1)^i(u_0,\ldots,\widehat u_i,\ldots,u_a)$ for $a>0$ and $\partial=0$ in degree zero; let $\epsilon_p:U(p)_0	o\mathbf Z$ send every vertex to $1$. Define $U(q)$ in the same way. Let $V(p,q)_n$ be the free abelian group on coordinatewise weakly increasing strings of $n+1$ pairs in $[p]	imes[q]$, with the same alternating deletion differential, zero in degree zero, and augmentation $\epsilon_V$ sending each pair vertex to $1$. Repetitions are retained in all these groups.

For strings $u\in U(p)_a$, $v\in U(q)_b$, set $n=a+b$. For a partition $\mu\sqcup
u=\{0,\ldots,n-1\}$ with $|\mu|=a$, $|
u|=b$, put $A_k=\#\{j\in\mu:j<k\}$, $B_k=\#\{j\in
u:j<k\}$ for $0\leq k\leq n$. Write $\epsilon(\mu,
u)$ for the sign of the permutation obtained by listing $\mu$ and then $
u$, each increasingly. Define
$$\sigma(u\otimes v)=\sum_{\mu,
u}\epsilon(\mu,
u) ig((u_{A_0},v_{B_0}),\ldots,(u_{A_n},v_{B_n}) ig),$$
extended bilinearly, where $U(p)_a\otimes_{\mathbf Z}U(q)_b$ is equivalently the free abelian group on pairs $(u,v)$. Then
$$\partial\sigma(u\otimes v)=\sigma(\partial u\otimes v)+(-1)^a\sigma(u\otimes\partial v),\qquad \epsilon_V\sigma_0=\epsilon_p\otimes\epsilon_q.$$
The first identity omits the first term when $a=0$ and the second term when $b=0$. Every pair of monotone maps $[p]	o[p']$, $[q]	o[q']$ commutes with $\sigma$ by postcomposition on the entries.

proof.text: All groups and maps in the statement are defined on finite bases in each degree and extended linearly. Deletion preserves weak increase. For any string of degree at least two, deleting original positions $i<j$ in the two possible orders gives the same remaining string with coefficients $(-1)^{i+j-1}$ and $(-1)^{i+j}$, which cancel. The composite differential in degree one is zero by the degree-zero convention. Also the augmentation of the boundary of an edge is $1-1=0$. Thus the three displayed constructions are augmented chain complexes in the convention of [def-weil-pbc-module-chain-complex-homology]. For a shuffle, $A_k,B_k$ are nondecreasing and in the stated index ranges, so every summand is a valid generator of $V$.

source.place: Paragraph (3), agent-written universal shuffle boundary calculation; the blueprint motivates the comparison but supplies no combinatorial proof. The numbered cases below are proved directly from the displayed definitions.

proof.text: Encode a partition by a word $w$ of length $n=a+b$ with $a$ letters $H$ in the positions of $\mu$ and $b$ letters $V$ in those of $\nu$. Write $z(w)$ for its pair string and $I(w)$ for the number of pairs of positions in which a $V$ precedes an $H$. The concatenated permutation $(\mu,\nu)$ has precisely these inversions: each block is increasing and a cross-block inversion is a vertical position smaller than a horizontal position. Hence its sign is $s(w)=(-1)^{I(w)}$. For $n>0$, expansion of the left side of the boundary identity is the finite sum over labeled pairs $(w,k)$, $0\leq k\leq n$, of $s(w)(-1)^k$ times $z(w)$ with vertex $k$ omitted. We compare these labeled terms before collecting equal generators.

source.place: Paragraph (3), agent-written universal shuffle boundary calculation; the blueprint motivates the comparison but supplies no combinatorial proof. The numbered cases below are proved directly from the displayed definitions.

proof.text: Consider $0<k<n$ where letters $k-1,k$ of $w$ are different. Swap these two letters to obtain $w'$, keeping $k$ fixed. This is a fixed-point-free involution on these labeled pairs. Before the two moves and after the two moves the lattice vertices agree; their only possibly different vertex is the deleted vertex $k$. Thus the surviving pair strings agree entry by entry, including when $u$ or $v$ has repetitions. Only the inversion between the two adjacent letters changes, so $s(w')=-s(w)$. The coefficients $s(w)(-1)^k$ and $s(w')(-1)^k$ therefore cancel pairwise.

source.place: Paragraph (3), agent-written universal shuffle boundary calculation; the blueprint motivates the comparison but supplies no combinatorial proof. The numbered cases below are proved directly from the displayed definitions.

proof.text: Suppose instead that $0<k<n$ and both neighboring letters are $H$. Put $i=A_k$ and $t=B_k$, so $k=i+t$ and $1\leq i<a$. Remove the vertex between the two horizontal moves and replace those two letters by a single $H$, giving a word $\bar w$ with $a-1$ horizontal letters and $b$ vertical letters. The deleted pair string is exactly the $\bar w$ summand for $(u_0,\ldots,\widehat u_i,\ldots,u_a)$ and $v$. One of the two identical horizontal moves has been removed; its inversions are the $t$ preceding vertical moves. Hence $I(w)=I(\bar w)+t$, and $s(w)(-1)^k=s(\bar w)(-1)^{t+i+t}=s(\bar w)(-1)^i$. For each fixed $i$ and each such $\bar w$ the inverse operation splits its $i$-th horizontal move (counted from one) into two horizontal moves; this gives exactly one labeled pair $(w,k)$.

source.place: Paragraph (3), agent-written universal shuffle boundary calculation; the blueprint motivates the comparison but supplies no combinatorial proof. The numbered cases below are proved directly from the displayed definitions.

proof.text: The horizontal endpoints give the missing horizontal faces. If $k=0$ and the first letter is $H$, remove that letter; no inversion is removed, and the remaining string is the shuffle of $(u_1,\ldots,u_a)$ with $v$. Its coefficient is $s(\bar w)$, the face sign for $i=0$. If $k=n$ and the last letter is $H$, remove that letter; it has all $b$ vertical letters before it, so $I(w)=I(\bar w)+b$ and $s(w)(-1)^n=s(\bar w)(-1)^{b+a+b}=s(\bar w)(-1)^a$. The remaining string is the shuffle of $(u_0,\ldots,u_{a-1})$ with $v$. Prepending or appending $H$ gives the inverse bijection with the shorter shuffle words. For $a=1$ there are no interior horizontal faces, and these two distinct labeled endpoint cases still apply; for $a=0$ there are no horizontal cases at all.

source.place: Paragraph (3), agent-written universal shuffle boundary calculation; the blueprint motivates the comparison but supplies no combinatorial proof. The numbered cases below are proved directly from the displayed definitions.

proof.text: If $0<k<n$ and the two neighboring letters are $V$, put $i=A_k$, $j=B_k$, so $k=i+j$ and $1\leq j<b$. Collapse the two vertical moves to one, obtaining $\bar w$ with $a$ horizontal letters and $b-1$ vertical letters. The surviving string is its shuffle on $u$ and $(v_0,\ldots,\widehat v_j,\ldots,v_b)$. The removed vertical move has exactly $a-i$ horizontal moves after it; hence $I(w)=I(\bar w)+a-i$. Consequently $s(w)(-1)^k=s(\bar w)(-1)^{a-i+i+j}=s(\bar w)(-1)^{a+j}$. For each fixed $j$ and shorter word, splitting its $j$-th vertical move (counted from one) recovers the unique original labeled pair.

source.place: Paragraph (3), agent-written universal shuffle boundary calculation; the blueprint motivates the comparison but supplies no combinatorial proof. The numbered cases below are proved directly from the displayed definitions.

proof.text: At $k=0$ with first letter $V$, removal of that letter removes $a$ inversions. The remaining string is the shuffle on $u$ and $(v_1,\ldots,v_b)$ with coefficient $s(\bar w)(-1)^a$, as required for $j=0$. At $k=n$ with last letter $V$, no inversion is removed. The remaining string is the shuffle on $u$ and $(v_0,\ldots,v_{b-1})$ with coefficient $s(\bar w)(-1)^{a+b}$, as required for $j=b$. Prepending or appending $V$ is the inverse bijection. For $b=1$ these are the only vertical cases, and for $b=0$ there are none.

source.place: Paragraph (3), agent-written universal shuffle boundary calculation; the blueprint motivates the comparison but supplies no combinatorial proof. The numbered cases below are proved directly from the displayed definitions.

proof.text: For $n>0$ these cases exhaust the expanded left side: an endpoint has a first or last letter of exactly one type, and an interior vertex has either different neighbors or two horizontal or two vertical neighbors. After the mixed terms cancel, the horizontal bijections give precisely $\sum_{i=0}^a(-1)^i\sigma((u_0,\ldots,\widehat u_i,\ldots,u_a)\otimes v)$ when $a>0$, while the vertical bijections give precisely $\sum_{j=0}^b(-1)^{a+j}\sigma(u\otimes(v_0,\ldots,\widehat v_j,\ldots,v_b))$ when $b>0$. This is the asserted boundary identity. No injectivity of the evaluation of labeled strings was used. If $n=0$, both boundaries and both omitted terms are zero. Equality on basis pairs extends bilinearly to all elements.

source.place: Paragraph (3), agent-written universal shuffle boundary calculation; the blueprint motivates the comparison but supplies no combinatorial proof. The numbered cases below are proved directly from the displayed definitions.

proof.text: In degree zero $a=b=0$ and the unique word is empty, with sign $1$; $\sigma_0$ sends the pair of vertices $(u_0,v_0)$ to that pair vertex. Both $\epsilon_V\sigma_0$ and $\epsilon_p\otimes\epsilon_q$, under $\mathbf Z\otimes_{\mathbf Z}\mathbf Z\cong\mathbf Z$, take every such basis pair to $1$. Linearity proves the augmentation identity.

source.place: Paragraph (3), agent-written universal shuffle boundary calculation; the blueprint motivates the comparison but supplies no combinatorial proof. The numbered cases below are proved directly from the displayed definitions.

proof.text: For monotone $f:[p]\to[p']$ and $g:[q]\to[q']$, the shuffle term indexed by $w$ after postcomposition has vertex $(f(u_{A_k}),g(v_{B_k}))$. This is exactly the $w$ term obtained by first postcomposing $u,v$ and then shuffling; the indexing words and signs do not change. Summing proves naturality. Postcomposition also commutes entry by entry with deletion and sends a vertex to a vertex, so these are maps of the augmented complexes. Noninjective maps can identify generators, but equality term by term before collecting coefficients remains valid.
